slides.title: Iterator Categories Overview
slides.prompt: Iterators act as a bridge between STL algorithms and containers. C++ defines five main iterator categories: Input, Output, Forward, Bidirectional, and Random Access, each providing specific capabilities.

slides.title: Advancing Iterators
slides.prompt: Fill in the function used to safely advance an iterator by n positions.
slides.codeSnippet:
auto it = vec.begin();
std::___(it, 3); // Moves iterator forward by 3 steps

slides.prompt: Fill in the function that calculates the number of elements between two iterators.

slides.title: std::next vs std::advance
slides.prompt: What is the key functional difference between std::next and std::advance?
options: std::next returns a new iterator without modifying the original; std::advance modifies the iterator in-place
std::advance works only on forward lists; std::next works on vectors
std::next advances in linear time; std::advance is always constant time
There is no difference; they are aliases for each other
slides.correctAnswer: std::next returns a new iterator without modifying the original; std::advance modifies the iterator in-place

slides.title: Getting Previous Iterator
slides.prompt: Fill in the function that returns an iterator decremented by n positions.

slides.title: Output Iterators Requirement
slides.prompt: Which of the following describes the primary behavior of an Output Iterator?
options: Allows single-pass writing to elements (e.g., std::back_inserter or std::ostream_iterator)
Allows multi-pass reading and writing in both directions
Supports random access via bracket operator []
Can read the same value multiple times without advancing
slides.correctAnswer: Allows single-pass writing to elements (e.g., std::back_inserter or std::ostream_iterator)
